blocks.text: Warmup gradually increases the learning rate from a very low starting value up to its intended target value over the first portion of training, rather than starting training at full learning rate from the very first step, a small technique that meaningfully improves training stability.
This topic explains why starting at full strength immediately can be risky, and how warmup addresses that risk before handing off to the decay schedule covered in the next topic of this module.
1. What Warmup Means in Training

blocks.alt: A low learning rate gradually rises to the target learning rate

blocks.text: During the warmup phase, the learning rate starts very small and increases gradually, often linearly, over a set number of early training steps, only reaching its full intended value once the warmup period ends.
2. Why Starting at Full Learning Rate Can Be Risky

blocks.alt: Full learning rate from step zero risks large, unstable early updates

blocks.text: Early in training, before the model has settled into a reasonable region of its weight space for the new task, gradients can be large or somewhat erratic, and applying the full intended learning rate to those early, potentially noisy gradients risks pushing the weights too far in an unhelpful direction before training has had a chance to stabilize.
3. The Warmup Schedule Shape

blocks.alt: Step one starts at a very low learning rate, rising by step fifty, and reaching the target by step one hundred

blocks.text: A typical warmup schedule increases the learning rate linearly from near zero up to the target value over a fixed number of steps, though other shapes are used too, the key property is a gradual, controlled ramp rather than an abrupt jump straight to full strength.
4. How Long Warmup Typically Lasts

blocks.alt: A short warmup is compared against a longer warmup

blocks.text: Warmup periods are typically a small fraction of total training, often just a few hundred steps or the first few percent of total training steps, long enough to stabilize early training without eating meaningfully into the time spent at the full target learning rate.
5. Warmup and Random Initial Weights

blocks.alt: Randomly initialized layers benefit most from warmup

blocks.text: Warmup matters most for any part of a model still carrying randomly initialized weights, since those weights have no useful structure yet and are especially sensitive to large early updates, a consideration relevant to methods like LoRA, covered in the earlier module, where the newly added matrices start from near random initialization even though the base model itself is already pretrained.
6. Warmup Specific to Fine-Tuning

blocks.alt: Already pretrained weights often need less warmup

blocks.text: Because fine-tuning starts from an already pretrained model, rather than random weights throughout, warmup periods for fine-tuning tend to be shorter than those used during full pretraining from scratch, since most of the model already sits in a stable, well trained region of weight space.

blocks.title: This connects directly to the Pretraining vs Fine-Tuning topic
blocks.content: Just as fine-tuning needs far less data and compute than pretraining because it starts from an already capable model, it also typically needs a shorter warmup period for the same underlying reason.

blocks.text: 7. What Happens Without Warmup

Skipping warmup entirely and starting straight at full learning rate can produce visibly unstable early training, a loss curve that spikes or behaves erratically in the first steps before eventually settling down, if it settles down at all, sometimes derailing a training run altogether.
8. Warmup Combined With a Decay Schedule

blocks.alt: A warmup phase leads into a decay phase, together forming the full training schedule

blocks.text: Warmup is almost always paired with a decay schedule, covered directly in the next topic of this module, together forming the complete learning rate trajectory across an entire training run, ramp up carefully at the start, hold or gradually reduce for the remainder.
9. Choosing a Warmup Length in Practice

A reasonable starting point sets warmup to somewhere between one and ten percent of total training steps, adjusting upward if early training still looks unstable at that setting, or downward if warmup seems to be taking up an unnecessarily large share of the total training budget without adding a visible stability benefit.
Worked Example
A team fine-tuning with LoRA notices their loss spikes sharply in the first several training steps before recovering, a telltale sign of an unstable start given their newly initialized LoRA matrices.

Adding a warmup period covering the first five percent of their total training steps smooths out this early instability entirely, the loss now decreases steadily from the very first step instead of spiking, confirming the earlier instability was specifically a warmup related issue rather than a deeper problem with their data or configuration.
Common Mistakes

items: Skipping warmup entirely and being surprised by unstable early training loss
Setting warmup far too long, eating unnecessarily into the portion of training spent at full learning rate
Assuming fine-tuning needs the same warmup length as full pretraining from scratch, when it typically needs less
Not connecting an unstable early loss curve back to a missing or too short warmup period as a likely cause

blocks.text: Practice

For a training run of one thousand total steps, calculate what a five percent warmup period would look like in terms of number of steps, and sketch roughly how the learning rate would rise during that period before reaching its target value.
Key Takeaway

Warmup gradually raises the learning rate from a low starting value up to its target over the earliest portion of training, protecting against unstable, potentially damaging large updates before the model has settled into a stable training trajectory, and it typically needs a shorter period for fine-tuning than for full pretraining from scratch.
